body_markdown:
To stop revenge bedtime procrastination, keep the me time and change how it ends. Notice the moment you're still scrolling but no longer enjoying it, take 30 seconds of gentle 4-6 breathing (in for 4, out for 6), then switch to a calm last thing you chose ahead of time.

This works with you instead of against you. The evening that's finally yours isn't the problem. The feed is. It keeps your body on alert long after you meant to wind down, which is how you end up tired and wired at once.

## What is revenge bedtime procrastination?

Revenge bedtime procrastination means staying up later than you planned, with nothing actually stopping you from going to bed, because late night feels like the only time that belongs to you. Researchers call the core behavior [bedtime procrastination](/glossary/#bedtime-procrastination) and leave out the "revenge" part.

The research term comes from a 2014 Dutch paper. It defined bedtime procrastination as [failing to go to bed at the intended time while no external circumstances prevent you from doing so](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24994989/). In that first study of 177 people, lower self-regulation went with more bedtime procrastination, and bedtime procrastination predicted insufficient sleep. A follow-up asked [more than 2,000 Dutch participants (aged 16 to 93) to keep a 7-day sleep diary and found bedtime procrastination explained 12.7% of the variation in their sleep](https://www.bps.org.uk/research-digest/psychologists-investigate-major-ignored-reason-our-lack-sleep-bedtime). Both studies were correlational, so they show a link but can't prove cause.

The "revenge" label is newer. It [began as a Chinese expression and spread in English during the COVID-19 pandemic](https://www.psychologytoday.com/nz/blog/sleepless-in-america/202106/what-is-revenge-bedtime-procrastination). It captures the feeling well: the day took your time, so you take some back at night. But it's popular usage, not a clinical category or a diagnosis.

The research field is young. The term itself only dates to that 2014 paper, so most of what we know comes from the last decade or so of studies, and much of it is still observational.

### How is it different from insomnia?

With insomnia, you go to bed and can't fall asleep or stay asleep. With bedtime procrastination, you probably could sleep. You just aren't in bed yet. The two can overlap, though. Night after night, the lost sleep can leave you with [daytime sleepiness and fatigue](https://www.psychologytoday.com/nz/blog/sleepless-in-america/202106/what-is-revenge-bedtime-procrastination), which is a good reason to deal with it early.

## Why do you stay up late even when you're exhausted?

You stay up because late evening is often the first part of the day when nobody needs anything from you, and by then the self-control you'd use to stop is running low. That's a reasonable wish meeting a tired brain. It isn't a personal failing.

A [2022 meta-analysis of 43 studies](https://www.pubmed.gov/36375334/) found moderate links between bedtime procrastination and lower self-control and an evening chronotype (a body clock that runs late). It also found links with shorter sleep, poorer sleep quality and daytime fatigue. The authors rated the overall quality of the evidence as low on the GRADE scale and point out that studies testing cause and effect are still needed.

One finding stands out. In a 2018 study by Kamphorst and colleagues, [people who reported resisting more desires during the day also reported more bedtime procrastination](https://www.psychologytoday.com/nz/blog/sleepless-in-america/202106/what-is-revenge-bedtime-procrastination). A day full of "not now" (no to the snack, no to the nap, no to the sharp reply to a colleague) seems to leave less in the tank for "time for bed."

Your circumstances matter too. The Sleep Foundation calls it an [emerging concept linked to daytime stress and long work hours](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-hygiene/revenge-bedtime-procrastination), with several factors working together. If your day is packed with obligations, of course you want a bit of time at the end of it.

## Is the phone the problem, or the evening?

The evening is fine. The feed is the problem. Wanting an hour to yourself is healthy. What stretches that hour into three is a feed with no natural end, one that keeps your attention moving and your body slightly braced.

Most of the research here is observational, but it points the same way. One study followed [1,181 Chinese college students for 12 months](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8431882/). Problematic phone use (the compulsive, hard-to-put-down kind) predicted poorer sleep quality a year later, and bedtime procrastination and poor sleep fed each other in both directions. In a study of Spanish adults, [problematic smartphone use was linked to worse sleep only indirectly, through bedtime procrastination](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10604906), with no direct effect. Put simply, the phone seems to cost sleep mostly by keeping people up past the time they meant to go to bed.

For the evening question, the most useful study is a small trial from 2019. [Sixty-four adults aged 18 to 29 spent 15 minutes each evening for 30 days either doing slow breathing (about 4.5 seconds in, 5.5 seconds out) or using social media](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6406675). The breathing group reported better sleep quality and had higher overnight [heart rate variability](/glossary/#heart-rate-variability), a common marker of the calming branch of the nervous system. The social media group didn't improve. The study was small, the participants were young, and sleep was self-reported, so take it as encouraging rather than settled.

For what the screen itself does (and why blue light isn't the whole story), see [is scrolling before bed bad?](/blog/is-scrolling-before-bed-bad/) For the wired-at-midnight feeling in particular, read [why you feel wired after doomscrolling at night](/blog/doomscrolling-at-night/).

## How to stop revenge bedtime procrastination mid-scroll: notice, reset, switch

The mid-scroll downshift has three steps. Notice when the scroll has stopped being enjoyable, reset with about 30 seconds of slow 4-6 breathing, and switch to a low-stimulation last thing you picked earlier. It's built for 11:40 pm, 40 minutes into the feed, which is exactly where most bedtime plans fall apart.

### 1. Notice: still scrolling, no longer enjoying it

Your cue is a feeling, not the clock. Common signs:

- Your jaw is tight or your shoulders have crept up toward your ears.
- Your thumb keeps moving, but you couldn't name the last three things you saw.
- You're rereading posts, or reopening the app you just closed.
- You feel a low hum of irritation, at the feed or at yourself.

That moment is your off-ramp. You don't have to be finished with your evening. You only have to notice that this part of it has stopped giving you anything.

### 2. Reset: 30 seconds of 4-6 breathing

Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 4. Then let the breath out slowly for a count of 6, through your nose or softly parted lips. Each breath takes about 10 seconds, so three breaths take about 30 seconds. Don't hold your breath and don't gulp air. It should feel like a long, unhurried sigh, not a lung workout. If you'd like something to pace you, our free [calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) runs in your browser.

This pattern is close to the one in the 2019 trial, with a slightly longer exhale. But be honest about the scale. No study has tested a 30-second reset on sleep. The trials used [15-minute sessions](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6406675) and [30-minute sessions](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7198497). The 30-minute study was a pilot with only 20 participants, and in it, breathing at 5 breaths per minute raised heart rate variability but didn't help people fall asleep faster. So use the reset as a way to change how you feel and break the scroll's momentum, not as a sleep fix. If you like it, you can stretch it to 5 or 10 minutes once you're in bed.

This is the moment DeRot is built for. It meets you mid-scroll and pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths, so you come down while you're still in the moment instead of only after you finally force the phone down. The goal is small: your shoulders drop and the next video loses some of its pull. (DeRot is launching soon on iOS.)

### 3. Switch: a low-stimulation last thing you chose

Choose your last thing earlier in the evening, while you have more self-control. Then at 11:40 you only have to pick from a short list instead of coming up with a plan. Some good options:

- A few pages of a paper book or e-reader
- Five minutes of stretching on the floor
- Herbal tea with the lights low
- A podcast or audiobook on a sleep timer
- A warm shower

The best last thing is one you actually enjoy. It's still your me time, just a version that lets your body come down.

### Common mistakes

- **Forcing big breaths.** Overbreathing can make you lightheaded. Keep it soft and quiet.
- **Using the reset as permission to keep going.** It's easy to feel calmer and then scroll for another hour. If you catch yourself doing that, go straight to your last thing.
- **Punishing yourself afterward.** Guilt winds you up too, and it tends to keep you awake. We cover this in [screen time guilt](/blog/screen-time-guilt/).
- **Waiting for a perfect night.** One downshift that works beats a strict plan you've dropped by Wednesday.

## Why an if-then check-in is more forgiving than a strict bedtime

A strict bedtime depends on willpower at the hour you have the least of it. An if-then plan attaches the decision to a cue you'll notice anyway. Early research on if-then plans alone is discouraging, so it makes sense to let your surroundings help too.

In a 2016 conference abstract, one research group reported that [if-then plans on their own hadn't reduced bedtime procrastination in their earlier work](https://www.ehps.net/ehp/index.php/contents/article/view/2169), and described testing them alongside environmental nudges, such as lamps that dim at the intended bedtime. That evidence is early and limited, so treat the combination as a sensible idea rather than a proven fix.

The practical lesson is to let the room do some of the work. Put a lamp on a timer, charge your phone across the room, and leave your book on your pillow. Each one makes the calm option the easy option at the moment you're least likely to choose it on willpower alone.

To write your own if-then line, think about the exact moment that usually derails you. For most people it's the "one more video" moment, not the decision to pick up the phone in the first place. Then write one sentence for that moment and nothing else.

Replace a hard bedtime with a check-in time:

> "When it's 10:45 and I'm still on the feed, I take three slow breaths and pick my last thing."

It's specific and forbids nothing. It asks you for 30 seconds, not a whole evening of resisting.

## A 60-second evening script you can use tonight

The whole script takes about a minute, and nothing is off-limits.

1. **Earlier in the evening (10 seconds).** Set a check-in alarm for 30 to 45 minutes before you want to be asleep. Give it a kind label, like "Still enjoying this?"
2. **When the alarm goes off (5 seconds).** Ask yourself whether you're enjoying this or just still here. If you're really enjoying it, that's fine. Set one more check-in for 15 minutes later.
3. **Three breaths (30 seconds).** In for 4, out for 6. Let your jaw loosen on each exhale.
4. **Choose your last thing (10 seconds).** Pick one from your list, then put the phone across the room or face down on its charger.
5. **If you end up back in the feed (5 seconds).** That's not a failure. Do one more reset, then go to your last thing.

## How to fix the daytime gap that steals your evenings

If late night is the only time that's yours, it will keep getting longer. Moving small pockets of me time into the day takes some of the pressure off midnight.

That could be a 10-minute walk at lunch with nothing in your ears, or 20 minutes to yourself after work before the chores start. It could also mean starting your wind-down at 9:30 so your own time doesn't begin at 10:45. Small daily pockets leave the evening with less to carry.

Lowering daytime stress helps as well. In one study, [108 people were randomly assigned to 5 minutes a day of one of several breathing practices or mindfulness meditation for 28 days](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947). [Cyclic sighing, which uses a long exhale, improved positive mood more than mindfulness](https://med.stanford.edu/news/insights/2023/02/cyclic-sighing-can-help-breathe-away-anxiety.html), but sleep measures didn't change significantly. You can try it with our [physiological sigh timer](/tools/physiological-sigh/).

The stakes are real, though not alarming. The CDC recommends [at least 7 hours of sleep a night for adults](https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/data-and-statistics/adults.html), and in 2024, [30.5% of US adults averaged less than 7 hours](https://cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db559.htm). Cleveland Clinic puts most adults' needs at [7 to 9 hours](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/revenge-bedtime-procrastination/).

## When is it more than bedtime procrastination?

If you go to bed and still can't sleep, or the pattern continues for more than a few weeks even after you've made changes, talk to a doctor. Cleveland Clinic advises [seeing a primary care provider if things don't improve after a few weeks](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/revenge-bedtime-procrastination/).

Also see a doctor or sleep specialist if you notice any of these:

- Trouble falling or staying asleep even when you go to bed on time
- Daytime sleepiness that affects your work or your driving
- Loud snoring, or gasping during sleep
- Low mood or anxiety that doesn't go away

A few notes on the breathing itself. Breathing exercises can help you feel calmer and may make winding down easier, but they won't fix insomnia or anxiety on their own. If you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly, stop and breathe normally. The 4-6 pattern has no breath holds, which is why we suggest it at bedtime. If you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic, skip patterns with holds, such as 4-7-8 or box breathing.

If staying up late is really about dreading tomorrow, or if you feel unsafe, please reach out now. Contact your local emergency services, or call or text 988 in the US.

faqs.question: Why is it called revenge bedtime procrastination?
faqs.answer: The "revenge" part comes from a Chinese expression that spread in English during the COVID-19 pandemic. The idea is that when work and obligations fill your day, you "get revenge" by staying up late to take some time back. Researchers just call the behavior bedtime procrastination, meaning going to bed later than you intended when nothing external is stopping you. "Revenge" is popular usage, not a clinical term.

faqs.question: Is revenge bedtime procrastination the same as insomnia?
faqs.answer: No. With insomnia, you go to bed and struggle to fall asleep or stay asleep. With bedtime procrastination, you could probably sleep, but you put off going to bed. The two can overlap, and short sleep night after night can leave you tired and foggy during the day. If you lie awake even when you go to bed on time, or poor sleep lasts more than a few weeks, talk to a doctor.

faqs.question: How long before bed should I stop using my phone?
faqs.answer: Cleveland Clinic suggests an hour without electronics before bed. That's a good target if it suits you, but all-or-nothing rules often fall apart by midweek. A gentler plan is to set a check-in alarm 30 to 45 minutes before you want to sleep. When it goes off, notice whether you're still enjoying the feed, take three slow breaths, then switch to a calm last thing. How you feel when you put the phone down matters most.

faqs.question: Can breathing exercises help me fall asleep?
faqs.answer: The evidence is mixed. In a 2019 trial, young adults who did 15 minutes of slow breathing each evening for 30 days reported better sleep quality, while a social media group did not. But a small 2020 pilot of 20 people found that 30 minutes of slow breathing raised heart rate variability without helping them fall asleep faster. Breathing can help you feel calmer and may make winding down easier, but it won't fix insomnia on its own.

faqs.question: Is scrolling in bed bad if it relaxes me?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. If you put the phone down feeling calm and fall asleep around the time you planned, it's working for you. The trouble starts when the scroll keeps going after the enjoyment has stopped: your jaw is tight, your thumb is on autopilot, and bedtime keeps slipping. Research suggests problematic phone use affects sleep mainly by keeping people up later, so watch both the clock and how you feel.

faqs.question: Does being a night owl make bedtime procrastination worse?
faqs.answer: It may. A 2022 meta-analysis of 43 studies found that bedtime procrastination was moderately linked to an evening chronotype, meaning a body clock that runs late. If 11 pm doesn't feel like bedtime to you, a strict early cutoff will probably fail. Set your check-in time around when you actually get sleepy, and leave room for the at least 7 hours of sleep the CDC recommends for adults.

howto_steps: Set a check-in alarm for 30 to 45 minutes before you want to be asleep.
When it goes off, ask whether you're enjoying the scroll or just still there.
Breathe in gently for 4 counts and out slowly for 6, three times (about 30 seconds), with no holds.
Pick the low-stimulation last thing you chose earlier, such as a book, stretches or a podcast on a sleep timer.
Put the phone across the room or face down on its charger.
If you drift back to the feed, do one more reset without judging yourself, then go to your last thing.
